summary: HotHub is an interactive web platform designed to harmonize NASA MODIS and VIIRS active fire records into a single, consistent monthly hot spot series for Indonesia from 2002 to today and beyond MODIS retirement. Using 24 years of thermal anomaly data from NASA GIBS (Aqua/Terra MODIS and Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 VIIRS) alongside aerosol optical depth records, our tool converts VIIRS detections into Aqua-equivalent units with an 80% uncertainty interval through a fire-size calibration model validated on hidden MODIS years. The platform empowers journalists, researchers, disaster management staff, and local residents to select any area, inspect monthly calendars against historical medians, and download transparent CSV records. HotHub addresses a critical challenge: existing fire counts differ across agencies and artificially surge as more satellites launch, while thick smoke can obscure active fires. By standardizing units, filtering persistent non-fire heat sources, and flagging smoke-obscured months, our tool enables reliable, apples-to-apples fire monitoring.
details:
1. The problem: the same fires, different numbers

Indonesian agencies already publish hot spot counts, but not one comparable series:

Source: Kompas, 7 September 2026:https://www.kompas.id/artikel/jangan-terfokus-pada-jumlah-titik-panas-dalam-penanganan-kebakaran-hutan-dan-lahan

Three things make the numbers drift apart:

  1. Thresholds differ. At BRIN, the same five days give 2,109 or 72,408 hot spots depending on the confidence level.
  2. Satellites are added together. One fire seen by three VIIRS satellites is counted three times, and the total jumps every time a satellite is launched.
  3. Sensors differ. VIIRS looks through 375 m pixels, MODIS through 1 km pixels, so VIIRS also finds small fires. A VIIRS count and a MODIS count are not the same unit.

And the long record is ending: the MODIS satellites are near the end of their missions, and Aqua's overpass time has been drifting since 2023.

2. What HotHub does

HotHub is a static web page. Pick an area (all of Indonesia, a preset province box, a point with a radius, or a drawn box) and a month. It shows:

  • A flat 3D pixel map of Indonesia on NASA Blue Marble, with one pillar per 0.1° cell (about 11 km). Pillar height is the hot spot count; colour ranks the month against the same month in other years. Click a pillar to read its cell. A slider and play button move through 292 months.
  • A month panel that leads with a verdict ("above normal", "near normal", "below normal"), then a picture, then the numbers: this month against the median and usual range of the same calendar month in earlier years.
  • A smoke rule. Thick smoke hides fires, so a low count under smoke is shown as "not trusted", never as "below normal". Smoke data starts 21 November 2015; earlier months say "no smoke data".
  • A monthly calendar (years by months), coloured by rank, with yearly totals.
  • A date range and CSV download: one row per month with the value, the interval, whether it was observed or estimated, and the smoke flag.
  • An explainer and a methods section with the test result, including what failed.

September 2015, all of Indonesia: 37,352 hot spots, the highest month in the record.

The "In real life" box turns the count into things a reader can picture. For September 2015 the page says: about 1,245 hot spots a day on average; heat seen in 5,387 map squares, 661,245 km² in all, about the size of Sumatra ("that is where fire was seen, not how much land burned"); the worst month in the record for this area. It adds one outside figure, with its source: in 2015, fires burned about 2.6 million hectares across Indonesia and cost about US$16.1 billion, by the World Bank's estimate.

August 2020: Aqua data is not usable this month, so the page shows the estimate rebuilt from Suomi NPP (3,251, likely between 2,719 and 4,030) and says so. Thick smoke was present, so the page refuses to call the low count good news. This is what every month will look like after MODIS ends.

3. How it works

Data. Every detection was fetched during the event from NASA GIBS vector tiles, without a key: 17,536 day files, 9.10 million detections, July 2002 to November 2026. No day failed.

One unit. The unit is the Aqua MODIS hot spot (confidence 30 or higher), per month. We chose Aqua because it has the longest record with one afternoon overpass, and people already quote MODIS-era numbers. A month without usable Aqua data is converted into the number Aqua would have reported.

Grid. Cells of 0.1°, blocks of 0.5°. Each satellite is kept apart (never pooled), and day and night are fitted apart, because the sensors differ most at night, when small cool fires are visible to VIIRS only.

Always-hot places removed. Gas flares, smelters and volcanoes are hot every day and are not fires. A cell with a detection on at least half of the days of a year, in at least three of the training years, is left out. 17 cells were found. The page names no facility or company.

Three candidate conversions.

Interval. The 10th and 90th percentiles of the training errors give an 80% interval. Errors are grouped by the size of the estimate, so large totals get narrower intervals.

Smoke flag. Daily aerosol optical depth at 550 nm (Meteomatics) at every 0.5° block. A smoke day has optical depth of 1.0 or more; a block-month with three or more smoke days is smoky. The flag never changes a count.

4. Does it work? The MODIS-denial test

We trained on 2012 to 2019, then hid Aqua for 2020 to 2022 and rebuilt it from Suomi NPP alone, and compared with what Aqua really saw. The pass criteria were written down before any result was seen:

  • C1: median absolute log error per block-month at most 0.9 times the baseline's.
  • C2: the 80% interval covers between 70% and 90% of the scored block-months.
  • C3: each test year's total within 25% of the real Aqua total.

95,817 training records; 19,336 scored block-months in the test years.

How to read this honestly:

  • The size model passes and is the one in use. Its pass on C1 is narrow: 0.2705 against a limit of 0.2727.
  • The monthly model fails and is reported as failed. Season alone does not explain the difference between the sensors; fire size does.
  • A median log error of 0.27 means a typical block-month estimate is off by about 30%. Small areas are uncertain; regional totals are much tighter.

From 2023 Aqua's overpass time drifts, so it is no longer a fair reference. Shown for information, the size model's yearly error is 0% in 2023, −7% in 2024, +5% in 2025 and −6% in 2026.

Red: what Aqua saw. Dashed: the same months rebuilt from Suomi NPP alone, with its 80% interval. The two lines overlap across 2012 to 2026, including the hidden test years.

Whole region. The page sums 0.1° cells, so its values differ from these regional totals by a few units (for example 3,251 instead of 3,236 for August 2020).

5. Case study: is 2026 worse than 2015?

Adding satellites together says 2026 was more than twice as bad as 2015. In one unit, January to October 2026 had about 80% of the hot spots of the same months in 2015, and September 2026 about 74%. The difference is the number of satellites in orbit, not the fires.

6. What it means on the ground

Hot spot counts are not burned area or damage, and HotHub does not claim they are. For the two worst years in the record, the page quotes the World Bank's own estimates next to the count:

7. Limits (reported as they are)

  • Only Suomi NPP is calibrated. NOAA-20 against Aqua failed C1, and its estimates for 2023 to 2026 are 13% to 27% too low. If Suomi NPP stops, the series stops until this is solved.
  • No cloud data. A cloudy month can look quiet. The smoke flag does not cover cloud.
  • Aerosol optical depth comes from a model product, at one time of day.
  • No field validation. Hot spots are heat anomalies seen by satellite, not confirmed fires.
  • The persistent-source rule is strict. Smaller or newer industrial sites remain in the counts.
  • Not near real time. The running month is shown only once it is complete.

8. Benefits and next steps

Who it helps:

  • Journalists, NGOs and researchers can say "this month is worse than usual" and defend the number, with one stated definition and a CSV.
  • Local government and disaster staff can compare this year with earlier fire years in the same unit.
  • Residents of fire-prone provinces get a plain-language verdict and a smoke warning.

HotHub is a complement to BMKG, SiPongi+ and BRIN, not a replacement.

Next steps:

  1. NOAA-20 standby: raw NOAA-20 and Suomi NPP counts agree closely in full years (ratio 0.98 to 1.06 in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2025 and 2026), so NOAA-20 could be converted to Suomi NPP first and then through the tested model. This would keep the series alive if Suomi NPP stops.
  2. Landsat cross-check through the NASA FIRMS API.
  3. Simple cards: haze now, and fires in the last 24 hours near a place.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (AI)

Code and documents were written with the help of an SI coding assistant (Claude, through Claude Code), directed and reviewed by the team. Commits made this way carry a Co-Authored-By line in the repository. The logo, the small pixel icons and the comic panels on the page are grids drawn in code with that assistant. No image on the page or on this project page comes from an image generator: the charts are rendered by code from the data pack, and the other images are screenshots of the page.
